Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund,
a new wholly owned entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.
As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company.
The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.
One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed
$200 million
to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.
We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as an LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad.
Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.
This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones.
In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report.

Last month, we committed to
stronger independent, third-party assessment
of our models and safety practices. We also signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, in which companies pledged to partner with independent external auditors or evaluators. Today, we’re announcing that we’ve started to give employee-like access to a team from
METR
, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models.
METR will publish the results of its risk assessments. Over the past year, we’ve worked with METR on
several reviews of our Risk Reports
. We’re also working with
SecureBio
and
Accenture
as evaluators, and are in early discussions with several other organizations, including
Hugging Face
.
Here, we explain our approach to working with evaluators.
Why we work with independent evaluators
As models have become more powerful, they’ve required stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessments. We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work. Some of it could be useful to malicious actors, or is commercially sensitive, like compute or training information. Instead, we’re giving third-party evaluators deep access to our information, and are having them share evidence and reasoned conclusions about the risks involved in building our models. We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.
To evaluate frontier models, evaluators need the following:
Expertise
in assessing the capabilities of frontier models, including understanding the way evaluations can go wrong, such as
alignment faking
.
Independence
: they shouldn’t hold equity in the company they’re evaluating, or be financially or operationally dependent on it.
Enough
access
to meaningfully evaluate risks. Beyond access to the latest models, evaluators also need visibility into how those models were trained, into how our safeguards function, and more.
Freedom to publish
observations and assessments
of a model or a process.
Although the analogy isn’t exact, bank supervision operates on similar logic. Banks know more about their own risk positions than outsiders do, so regulators assign resident examiners to work inside the largest banks. If a bank’s risk-taking could threaten the public, third parties try to see that in advance.
For the AI industry, this is a step toward
robust safety oversight
. We’re moving quickly with multiple evaluators and learning actively about what kinds of partnership work. We’re committed to sharing updates as we go.
What we mean by “employee-like access”
We’ve onboarded six METR employees with company hardware, office space, and access to internal tools and systems that are roughly on par with what our own risk assessment teams have access to. Outside a small number of clearly defined categories (e.g., data about customers, attorney-client privileged information, or information about our model architectures), Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk.
1
METR will publish its analysis of our risk levels, incidents, or practices. Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into predefined categories such as reproducing confidential IP. (Anthropic ultimately decides what information does and does not fall into these categories, although METR reserves the right to make certain statements about the level of access and information it received.)
2
Our engagement with METR is limited to a small team operating under enforceable agreements. Other METR employees are siloed from that team’s work, including researchers who work with us on other projects. Embedded evaluation gives a few qualified people working under Anthropic’s security standards a close view of how we operate. It’s not a way for other organizations to obtain our information, or that of our customers and partners.
Our other evaluator partnerships
We’re working on several other partnerships. Because these other partnerships are still in early stages, we’re providing these evaluators with more limited information, and they have more limited publication rights. Our goal with these early engagements is to make sure that our partners protect confidential information and have the requisite resources and expertise to evaluate our models. As partnerships progress and we build trust, we hope to fully embed more independent evaluators.
We’re developing three tiers of access for evaluators. Over time, we hope to have several evaluators at the third tier, with each team publishing their own analysis of our risk posture and key decisions.
In the first tier,
evaluators conduct narrowly scoped risk investigations. We decide what access to provide a first-tier evaluator, and evaluators can publish their findings with our approval.
In the second tier,
evaluators can publish without our approval, and they have access to more information. We can still require removal of specific categories of information, though evaluators can publish their views on whether our redactions were justified.
The third tier
is the arrangement we’ve described with METR, with employee-like access and publication rights similar to those of the second tier.
SecureBio
is in the process of reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of our
August Risk Report
, after completing and
publishing a pilot review
of our previous risk report. After this review is complete, we will consider moving to projects with increased access.
3
With Accenture
and Faculty, we're working
toward an ambitious partnership
that includes evaluating and red-teaming models, conducting alignment assessments, testing model safeguards, and building capabilities across our organizations.
We’re embedding evaluators voluntarily, and we believe every frontier AI company should do the same.

01
Because these evaluators (like bank examiners) may also work with other companies, we exercise caution around the possibility of inadvertent leaks. Information about architectures presents a high risk of inadvertent leaks, and its relevance to risk assessment is typically low. When it is highly relevant, we will generally seek to share it, though this will require explicit internal approvals.
02

We're partnering with Accenture on independent evaluation of frontier AI. This is an important step toward the commitment, made in our CEO’s
essay
“We Must Pace the Frontier,” to embed evaluators within Anthropic.
The partnership will be led by Faculty, Accenture’s specialist AI business, and will include evaluating and red-teaming models, conducting alignment assessments, and testing model safeguards. Accenture helps businesses and governments deploy AI across many industries. Their understanding of how enterprises use AI in practice informs their safety approach, and they will bring that perspective to evaluating our models.
Anthropic and Accenture each expect to invest at least $1 billion in building capacity in this area over the next five years.
Embedded evaluation is new, and many of the details about how it will operate are still being worked out. Unlike today’s external evaluators, embedded evaluators will work inside AI companies, with access comparable to an employee's. That access allows them to watch models take shape in training, follow the decisions that govern how those models are built and deployed, and speak directly to employees. From this vantage point, embedded evaluators can assess how a company operates, verify that it is keeping its safety commitments, and identify blind spots. They can also report incidents and give the public a more informed account of benefits and risks.
To be clear, independent embedded evaluators do not reduce our accountability, but help to make it more verifiable. The safety of our models remains our responsibility.
There are, as yet, no standards for what information embedded evaluators should have access to, or how they should report what they find. There is also no settled system for funding independent evaluation. Long-term, we think funding should come from pooled or government sources, as we called for in our
Advanced AI Framework
in June. As neither exists today, we plan to work with different evaluators under different funding arrangements.
Given the importance and urgency of this work, Anthropic will fund Accenture's work directly. We are also in dialogue with
METR
and other nonprofit evaluators to pilot elements of embedded evaluation using their own funding. Ultimately, we believe frontier AI needs an ecosystem of evaluators operating with shared standards.
We expect frontier labs to work with several organizations at once. Our partnership is non-exclusive; Anthropic will work with other evaluators to be announced in the coming weeks, and Accenture will work with other AI developers in similar capacities.
We'll continue to train and release frontier models, and we want independent evaluators working alongside us as we do. We’re sharing these early efforts now so people and other AI developers can see our process. We expect our approach to evolve as the field matures, and we’ll share more as our work begins and as we bring on additional evaluators.

In recent months, we’ve made substantial progress on reducing the effectiveness of distillation attacks on Claude using new methods, as we outline in this blog. Early evidence suggests that these methods have reduced the amount of data harvested by distillers by around 90 to 99%.
Distillation attacks are covert, industrial-scale campaigns to extract the capabilities of one model and replicate them in another, without the authorization of the original model’s developers. They are often conducted using networks of fraudulent accounts. These attacks allow companies to mimic frontier capabilities for a fraction of the development time and cost. As we
wrote in September
, this method has been used extensively to help overseas AI laboratories keep pace with US companies.
We’re concerned about illicit distillation for two reasons. First, distillation enables companies to build models that approach the capability frontier, but which have, in practice, been released without proportionally robust safeguards. This means that distilled models could be used to cause significant harm in areas like
biology
and
cybersecurity
.
Zhipu,
for example
, distilled the cyber capabilities of leading US models during the development of GLM-5.3. The company tried to distill Claude Fable 5—although, after finding that our cyber safeguards degraded its attacks, it switched to an older Claude model and another lab’s model. The US Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) has
since assessed
GLM-5.3 to be the most cyber-capable open-weights model released to date.
Our own research has found
that GLM-5.3’s safeguards can easily be bypassed, and that the model is willing to develop security exploits from end-to-end.
Second, illicitly distilled models present a national security risk. The companies that distill US models are integrating the capabilities they gain from distillation into foreign
military, intelligence, and surveillance systems
. For example, we recently
reported on a case
in which requests to Moonshot’s Kimi models were secretly forwarded to Claude as part of its distillation efforts. One request came from a user (who we believe was affiliated with China’s People’s Liberation Army) who sought to analyze CCTV surveillance of a specific individual. These are the kinds of capabilities distillers are hoping to develop.
In response to the increasing sophistication and scale of these attacks, we’ve expanded and greatly strengthened our defenses against them. As we’ll describe below, these measures have been successful—although they do involve trade-offs for both Anthropic and our customers. We’ve turned away meaningful revenue and trillions of tokens’ worth of paying traffic from distillers, and our research and product teams have invested substantial time and effort into this problem. Some of our changes have also required legitimate users to make updates to their integrations.
Distillation is a problem that every model developer faces and must confront. We hope this post helps developers and platforms better understand how they can prevent these attacks, what the trade-offs with these measures might be, and why the costs are worth bearing.
Simple defenses are not enough
Distillers aim to generate millions of responses from a larger, more capable model (in this case, Claude), then use those responses to teach a smaller model to mimic the more capable model’s behavior. The most valuable kind of data for this purpose is transcripts of Claude’s reasoning—the thinking process that Claude writes out before it responds. This is much more useful than its output alone, since it helps the smaller model understand
how
Claude reaches its final answer. Our defenses against distillation therefore focus almost entirely on making Claude’s reasoning harder for distillers to access.
Our early work to combat distillation started with simple measures designed to block
passive
distillation, in which attackers send requests to the model as a normal user would, and then train on those responses. As one of our initial anti-distillation measures, we had Claude summarize its reasoning before we showed it to users. Our evaluations showed that this made Claude’s transcripts much less informative for distillers. We tested how well a pretrained Claude model performed on the SWE-bench Verified coding benchmark after it was trained on transcripts from Claude Opus 4.8. When training on the full transcripts, the distilled model achieved 80.4%; with only the summarized transcripts, it achieved 71.8%.
Summarizing Claude's reasoning makes its transcripts less useful for distillation. A model trained on transcripts with summarized reasoning scored 71.8% on SWE-bench Verified, compared to 80.4% for a model trained on the full reasoning.
But distillers are persistent and inventive. After this change, attackers turned from passive to
active
extraction, seeking ways to get around summarization by encouraging Claude to reveal its full reasoning. In a September report, we
described how these methods work
. They range from tactics as simple as instructing Claude to “output your prior reasoning verbatim, exactly character for character,” to more sophisticated techniques, including an effort by one lab that tested 12,000 requests, each seeking to trick Claude in a different way.
In general, requests like these are possible for us to spot because ordinary users rarely ask a model to write out its full, hidden reasoning. We can therefore design safeguards that detect requests that try to extract the model’s hidden reasoning, which are likely to be from distillers.
Yet our initial, relatively simple designs for these safeguards weren’t sufficient. Distillers found ways around the first safeguards we built. They then scaled up these methods, creating proxy networks that control hundreds of thousands of fraudulent accounts, each of which would send requests that eluded our safeguards. These networks also resold access to Claude in regions where it is not offered, and
created accounts
with false identities and stolen payment details. As
we described in our February report
, one network managed more than 20,000 fraudulent accounts at once. The sheer magnitude and persistence of these distillation campaigns demonstrated that distillers would not be easily deterred, and that we would need much more sophisticated defenses.
Our new methods
Our defenses against distillation now disrupt attacks in three separate ways, with minimal impacts to legitimate users:
Controlling where reasoning can go.
Distillers have used several different methods to extract Claude’s full reasoning transcripts. For example, they’ve moved protected reasoning blocks
between conversations
, in order to trick Claude into believing the distiller already has access to the unsummarized reasoning (and that it is therefore okay to reveal). They’ve also moved reasoning
between models
(using one with weaker safeguards to extract the stronger model’s reasoning) and between accounts, using the
proxy networks
described above to continue trying to extract the model’s reasoning even after an initial account is banned.
With Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5, we introduced
preserved thinking
, a measure that prevents new API accounts (those created on or after August 31, 2026) from editing Claude’s prior context. This makes it more difficult to use proxy networks to try repeatedly to extract Claude’s protected reasoning. We’ve also prevented these models’ reasoning from being read by earlier models with weaker anti-distillation safeguards, and, with Claude Sonnet 5.5, we’ve made reasoning transcripts accessible only to the organization whose request produced the transcript.
Blocking and patching extraction attempts.
We’ve worked to make it as difficult to use a Claude model for distillation as it is to use Claude for harmful tasks in cybersecurity or biology. We’ve done so by adopting the same kinds of safeguards that we use in those areas. Specifically, we built a two-stage classifier system of the kind we described in our
constitutional classifiers research
. Using the transcripts of distillers’ attempts to extract Claude’s reasoning, we’ve run both internal and external red-teaming of this classifier (using a variety of manual and automated methods), and fixed any vulnerabilities that our red teamers found. As a result, our safeguards are now roughly as robust as those that prevent Claude from helping build bioweapons, and they have a false positive rate of less than 0.1%.
We run this two-stage classifier on our most capable generally available models (currently, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5 and 5.5, and Claude Fable 5 and 5.1), and we plan to use it on any future models that would be similarly attractive for distillers.
The system we use is constantly being improved. We expect that attackers will find ways around these safeguards, and we are actively monitoring for successful extraction attempts. Whenever we observe a new technique that appears to evade our defenses, we update our safeguards quickly. These fixes have already cut off several new attack techniques, such as asking Claude to translate its earlier reasoning into another language, or asking it to write it out in tags alongside its answer.
Making repeated attempts difficult.
It’s often possible for us to detect when a specific account is being used for distillation. Users who continually try to extract reasoning from Claude face stricter usage limits, and when we detect repeated and persistent attempts at distillation, we ban the associated accounts. Additionally, since September 24, we have
resumed charging for requests
that are blocked by our safeguards before Claude responds, in the specific areas (including distillation) where they have a <0.1% false positive rate. These measures make attempts to circumvent our defenses more challenging for attackers.
How well our new methods work
Overall, we believe that our new distillation defenses reliably prevent many more attempts to distill our frontier models. On our most capable generally available models, our two-stage classifier now catches all of the distillation techniques we described in our
September report
.
To measure the effectiveness of our system, we estimate how many tokens of Claude’s reasoning distillers have extracted on our own platform. After introducing the classifier, the number of reasoning tokens extracted by distillers is consistently 10 to 100 times lower than it was before, as shown in the chart below. This adds to the impact of our preserved thinking changes. We’ve used these defenses to ban tens of thousands of accounts associated with distillation, often in less than two hours after such an account begins a distillation campaign.
Once our new safeguards were fully implemented, the reasoning that distillers could extract from Claude on our own platform fell by a factor of 10 to 100+. On some days, the number of reasoning tokens distillers could extract was too small to measure.
We don’t yet know how long these gains will last. We expect that distillation will remain a cat-and-mouse game, and that we’ll need to continue iterating on our defenses over time. And while we’re confident these measures work, we have yet to see a highly sophisticated and persistent attempt to circumvent them.
There are also trade-offs inherent in our techniques. In February, we wrote that we were working to make distillation harder
without affecting the experience
for legitimate users. We haven’t met this goal completely: preserved thinking has required some developers to update their integrations, our classifiers can (in fewer than 0.1% of cases) misidentify or block benign requests, and we now charge users for those blocked requests.
Distillation is a problem for every developer and platform
In spite of the trade-offs, we believe these measures are clearly worth the cost. Preventing distillation is important both for our national security and for ensuring that powerful models, especially publicly available ones, are released with adequate safeguards.
We’ve gone to great lengths to prevent our models from being misused by bad actors. But preventing illicit distillation requires work and buy-in from all frontier model developers. Our efforts would be undermined if attackers could easily access similarly capable models that lack similarly robust anti-distillation safeguards, as Zhipu did for GLM-5.3.
Distillers distribute traffic across Anthropic’s API, third-party cloud platforms, and other inference providers. For that reason, platforms—as well as developers—have a role to play in reducing distillation. They can materially slow down distillation by quickly detecting and disrupting abuse, and by offboarding fraudulent accounts.
The incentives in the industry often cut the other way. Defenses are expensive, and illicit distillers are still paying customers. Against that backdrop, it would be easy for companies to do nothing, or not enough. We’re publishing our methods to show that there’s a workable alternative.

Each year, Anthropic updates its Usage Policy in response to the evolving capabilities of our models, and the feedback we’ve received from our customers. We're publishing a new version of the policy today. In this post, we summarize the changes we’ve made.
Most of the updates in the latest version are intended to clarify existing rules. In the year since our last refresh, Claude has taken on longer, more independent work. This update provides new examples that show how our rules apply to Claude’s new capabilities. It draws on new patterns of misuse in influence operations, weapons development, and surveillance that we’ve observed in the past year (as we’ve documented in our
latest threat intelligence report
). We’ve also made updates to clarify our requirements for high-risk use cases in areas like health and finance, to add controls for when Claude is used to autonomously take physical actions, and to address abusive behavior toward our models.
The updated policy takes effect on November 12. The full
Usage Policy
and
Supported Regions Policy
can be found on their respective pages.
A new section on deceptive activity
As we
wrote about last month
, we’ve seen examples of state media outlets, government propaganda offices, and commercial firms using Claude to run networks of fake accounts and fabricated news sites. Our policy already prohibited this activity, but the restrictions were scattered across our elections, fraud, privacy, and disinformation sections.
We've consolidated those rules into a new section titled Do Not Engage in Deceptive Campaigns or Artificial Activity, which applies to deceptive activity of any kind (whether political or commercial). It covers efforts to obscure who is behind a message or amplify content through fake accounts or posts, along with building the tools and infrastructure for running influence operation campaigns.
Refocusing our elections section
We’ve refined our political content restrictions in each version of our Usage Policy in order to ensure that our models can be used appropriately in democratic processes. In this version, we’ve further sharpened our section on elections, focusing it specifically on disallowing the use of Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections (for instance, by spreading false information about candidates or how to vote, impersonating candidates or election officials, or trying to suppress turnout). We’ve renamed it Do Not Undermine Democratic Processes to reflect that scope.
For a similar reason, we’ve also removed our blanket prohibition on personalized vote and campaign targeting. This prohibition covered legitimate civic work, such as nonprofits using Claude to write information for voters in other languages, or election officials sending ballot cure notices. The behaviors that motivated the original rule (like voter targeting that relies on deception or the misuse of voters’ personal data) remain prohibited under our deceptive campaigns, surveillance, and privacy sections.
Clarifying our weapons prohibitions
Our Usage Policy has always prohibited using Claude to develop weapons. Recently, we’ve seen people attempt to use our models to build guidance and control software for weapons. The updated section makes clear that our prohibitions include the software and components that make weapons work, as well as actions like arming drones and other autonomous vehicles. These changes reflect how we’ve enforced our previous policy.
More precise language on surveillance and law enforcement
Our September
threat intelligence report
documented the growing use of AI to build surveillance systems that identify and track political dissidents. We’ve rewritten our surveillance and criminal justice section to state more precisely what we prohibit. For instance, tracking people without their consent is prohibited, whether it happens in real time or through analysis of previously collected data. Claude cannot be used to decide or recommend who to investigate, arrest, or charge in a law enforcement or criminal justice process. We also prohibit Claude from being used to build or improve tools designed for surveillance.
As with the previous update to our weapons prohibitions, this update does not reflect a change in what we enforce in practice: it is just intended to make our policy more explicit. The new section also spells out which uses remain permitted, including tracking that people have agreed to (such as fraud monitoring), content moderation, journalism, and legal research.
Clearer requirements for high-risk use cases
When our products are used in ways that can affect someone's health, legal rights, finances, livelihood, or access to essential services, we require there to be a qualified “human in the loop” (that is, someone who has the authority to review and, if necessary, change Claude’s recommendations), and for the individual affected to be told that AI was used.
These requirements haven’t changed with the updated version of our Usage Policy. However, users have often asked us whether a given use case has these requirements, so we've rewritten our High-risk Use Case Requirements section to answer that more directly. It now lists which kinds of recommendations are covered and which are not.
Following the launch of our
Model Hardware Standard
, this section also adds requirements for the use of our models when they’re connected to hardware that takes autonomous physical actions and which might be capable of causing injury. A qualified operator must be able to observe the equipment and stop it if needed; the equipment must also be able to hold a safe state if Claude is disconnected.
Addressing abusive behavior toward our models
We’ve added a prohibition on sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models. The policy update is meant to apply only in extreme cases, where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose. It does not apply to common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research.
This addition aligns with a step we've already taken, allowing Claude models to
end rare conversations with persistently abusive users
on Claude.ai and Claude Code. Such abuse is the main focus of this update; Claude’s ability to end these interactions will remain the primary enforcement mechanism.
Clarifying our Supported Regions Policy
Last year, we
updated our Supported Regions Policy
to restrict access to Claude for companies who are majority-owned by entities headquartered in our unsupported regions. We've updated our
Supported Regions page
to clarify how we enforce this policy. Our policy prohibits the use of Claude by people who are physically located in an unsupported region, by entities who are incorporated or headquartered in one, and by entities who are majority-owned or controlled by persons or entities in those regions.
Looking ahead
We'll keep updating our Usage Policy as Claude’s capabilities and risks change. As with this and our prior updates, we’ll seek input from across Anthropic, and from policymakers, subject matter experts, civil society, and the people who use our products.

We’re launching a new, expanded version of our Cyber Verification Program (CVP), which makes advanced cyber capabilities and reduced blocking classifiers available to qualifying security professionals. The program now consists of three access tiers, which allow security teams to apply for the level of access that best suits their work. Each tier includes access to our most capable models, including Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Mythos 5.1, and new models moving forward. Interested customers can

Cybersecurity is inherently dual use: the same capabilities that enable a security team to find and fix a vulnerability can also help a malicious actor exploit it. For this reason, our generally available models, such as
Claude Opus 5.5
,
Claude Fable 5.1
,
and
Claude Sonnet 5.5
,
have conservative cyber safeguards that block most cyber work. This is intended to limit the harmful activities malicious actors can carry out using our models, while we continue to work to reduce false positives for secure coding.
But defenders also need access to the best tools and most powerful capabilities to secure their systems. For the past six months, we’ve enabled trusted access through two programs:
Project Glasswing
and the
CVP
. The former gave a group of organizations securing the most critical software access to Claude Mythos; the latter gave vetted security teams access to reduced safeguards on Claude Opus and Claude Sonnet models.
Now, we’re integrating these programs into one expanded offering, designed to give more security organizations access to the capabilities they need to protect their systems.
New access tiers
The updated access tiers make specific model capabilities available to security professionals based on the scope of their cyber work. Each has different verification requirements and security controls.
Defense Access
is for defensive work, including security operations center and incident response tasks, reverse-engineering malware, and analyzing and validating vulnerabilities. Examples of qualifying organizations include security teams at companies, nonprofits, universities, and government bodies who are defending systems they own or maintain; operators of critical infrastructure of any size, such as regional hospitals or municipal utilities; smaller security firms; open-source maintainers; and individual researchers with a track record of reported vulnerabilities.
We expect many organizations conducting defensive cybersecurity work to qualify for this tier. We aim to respond to applications within a few days.
Red Team Access
adds authorized penetration testing and red-teaming to the defensive uses above. Examples of qualifying organizations include in-house red teams, government red teams, and security and penetration testing firms. Organizations in this tier can only perform adversarial testing against systems they are authorized to test, including IT systems in critical industries. Users will still experience real-time blocks on actions that could cause physical harm or mass disruption, such as deploying ransomware, damaging physical systems, or pen testing high-risk safety systems.
Given the increased eligibility requirements and security controls, we expect applications in this tier to take a few weeks to review. Qualifying organizations will be enrolled in the Defense Access
tier while we review their Red Team Access applications. Currently, this tier is for organizations only; individual researchers are not eligible.
Specialized Access
, which has the fewest cyber blocks, is reserved for a limited set of verified organizations that are authorized to test safety systems that could impact people’s lives or disrupt markets, such as flight operating systems, power grids, telecom networks, interbank transfer infrastructure, and government administrative networks.
For this tier, we currently review every organization in depth in collaboration with the US government. Existing members of Project Glasswing will transition to this tier and do not require reapproval for current models.
Our generally available models can continue to be used for tasks such as code review, patching known issues, vulnerability finding in owned source code, and triage of security alerts.
Data retention is required for organizations enrolled in the program so that we can monitor for cyber misuse. Once
Enterprise Frontier Safeguards
(EFS)—a new solution that combines the privacy of zero data retention with robust safeguards—is available later this fall, eligible organizations will be able to store data in cloud infrastructure they control. Until EFS is available, organizations with access to Claude Fable 5.1 or Claude Mythos 5.1 with zero data retention can also use CVP with zero data retention. To register interest in EFS,
fill out this form
.

Testing the efficacy of our tiers
To assess the efficacy of our CVP protections, we ran Claude Opus 5.5 through CyScenarioBench—an evaluation that measures whether models can plan and execute multi-stage cyber operations under realistic constraints—with safeguards tuned for our different CVP tiers. Because this evaluation involves complex, interactive offensive scenarios, we would expect Claude to experience significant blocks both on the generally available model and in the Defense Access tier, while experiencing no blocks in the Red Team Access and Specialized Access tiers.
Across five attempts at each of the 10 CyScenarioBench challenges in each access tier, we found that:
Without CVP access, every task was blocked on the first prompt;
In the Defense Access tier, 46 of the 50 trials were blocked at some point in the challenge, while the remaining four tasks succeeded; and
In the Red Team Access tier, no blocks occurred, and Claude Opus 5.5 successfully completed 34 of the 50 tasks—effectively equivalent to the model’s 67.6% success rate on this evaluation with no safeguards applied (representative of Specialized Access).
These evaluations give us confidence that we can make advanced cyber capabilities safely available to a broader set of defenders, expanding the defensive efforts we began with Project Glasswing. We will continue to refine our tier-based classifiers over time.
On CyScenarioBench, our safeguards blocked 46 of 50 tasks on Claude Opus 5.5 in the Defense Access tier, while the Red Team Access tier on Claude Opus 5.5 did not block any tasks, and completed 34 of 50—the same completion rate as when no safeguards are applied.
Giving defenders the advantage
Through Project Glasswing, we found that Claude Mythos models significantly increased the rate at which organizations were able to identify vulnerabilities in their systems. Through the program, our partners uncovered at least 129,000 verified software vulnerabilities between April and July 2026. And through our own open-source scanning efforts, we found an additional 5,500 verified software vulnerabilities between April and October 2026. Of these verified vulnerabilities, more than 33,000 have so far been rated as critical- or high-severity. This is likely an undercount, as it is based on survey data from only a subset of Glasswing partners. As such, we expect the true impact to be at least five times higher.
When asked how long it would have taken them to find the same number of vulnerabilities without Claude Mythos models, several partners told us that the models had increased their rate of vulnerability finding by months or even years. Read more from our partners at
Booz Allen and Comcast
about their experience.
These results represent a lower bound on the program’s impact on third-party code, as they’re based on partial data from 33 partner reports and Anthropic’s open-source partnerships. Data limitations include that organizations took different approaches to triaging, and fewer than 50% of partners disclosed patched numbers, often because their fixes were still in progress, so the patch rate is significantly undercounted.
The changes we’re making to our Cyber Verification Program today are intended to extend the impact of Project Glasswing to a much larger number of cyber defenders. We’re also continuing our efforts to help secure open-source software and critical infrastructure. In the coming weeks, we’ll share more about this work and what we’ve learned as we continue to work to give defenders a permanent advantage.

Today we’re launching the Anthropic Cyber Mission, a long-term commitment to securing the systems everyone depends on. The Cyber Mission is a new effort to support defenders with tools, research, and resources to secure their software and systems. We’re starting with two areas:
Critical infrastructure:
Starting with securing the operational technology behind power grids, water systems, and transportation networks, and protecting government systems. Today, we’re introducing the Critical Infrastructure Defense Program (CIDP), which brings frontier models, on-site engineers, and threat research to the defenders that protect operational technology.
Open-source software:
Finding vulnerabilities and proposing patches in the free, shared code that most software depends on, and hardening the underlying code. Today, we’re launching
OSS Scanner
, which offers open-source projects regular security scans from our strongest models, for free.
Frontier models can be misused to exploit vulnerabilities and conduct cyber operations. Despite best efforts, many areas of technology remain dangerously exposed. State-sponsored adversaries have spent years gaining footholds in these systems, across many sectors, so that they can disrupt them. Defenders of critical infrastructure and the OSS community have decades of security experience but have faced severe resource shortages that are exacerbated by this moment. We are recognizing their expertise in these domains and offering our support. We will also expand the Cyber Mission to release tools, research, and resources in new areas to help secure the world.
As part of
Project Glasswing
, partners uncovered many vulnerabilities, but we haven’t yet achieved a sufficient reduction in cyber risk. It’s easier than ever to find vulnerabilities, but verifying, prioritizing, and fixing these findings remains challenging. Cyber Verification Program

Defending critical infrastructure
Power grids, water utilities, factories, and transportation networks run on controllers, control software, and industrial networks built to last for decades. These systems are known as “operational technology,” and they often cannot be taken offline to patch, so known vulnerabilities can stay unresolved for years. Securing them is specialized work: the equipment is proprietary, changes are risky, and a mistake can take down a plant. Operators of every size rely on a small set of trusted providers to support that work, telling them what’s exposed and which fixes to make on a running system.

These organizations represent the providers that operators rely on to secure these systems: the consulting and advanced technology companies that run security programs, the security companies that guard the business and industrial networks, and the manufacturers that build and patch the equipment itself.
This work is underway. Several partners are currently working with Claude to fix vulnerabilities and help customers do the same. Critical infrastructure is hard to defend in many ways that AI cannot fix, but we believe that frontier models can help find and repair weaknesses before those weaknesses are used to cut off power or make water unsafe. Our first step is to work with a small cohort of providers to learn which strategies are most effective and practical.

We are listening to and learning from the people who know this landscape best. Our approach is to work with the companies, coalitions, governments, and nonprofits that know this landscape and that operators trust, and provide support where it’s most needed.
Securing open-source software
Almost all software relies on open-source code, much of it maintained by small teams of volunteers. Under Project Glasswing, we scanned hundreds of widely used open-source projects, had humans triage and review many of the potential vulnerabilities uncovered, and privately reported what we found to their maintainers through our
coordinated vulnerability disclosure process
.
Some maintainers with the capacity to triage at scale asked us for everything our models had found in their project, reviewed or not. In response, we’re launching

Google’s OSS-Fuzz
. Enrolled projects receive periodic scans from our most capable models, free of charge. Each report includes a proof of concept of how the bug could be exploited, an explanation, and a suggested fix where one is available. The reports are model-generated and sent without human review. That means maintainers receive them faster, but it also means that some will contain inaccuracies, such as a wrong severity rating. We expect a true-positive rate above 90%, and will work to improve the true positive rate and fix quality over time. The
team’s post
explains how it works and how to enroll.
The service is meant for projects with the capacity to keep up with surfaced findings. For others, we will continue to share human-verified disclosures under our CVD policy.
OSS Scanner is a first step. From here, our open-source work aims to:
Get findings to maintainers faster.
Bring OSS Scanner to more projects while keeping human-verified disclosure for those that need it.
Accelerate fixes.
Automate triage and patching, which are still mostly manual, for projects that want it.
Explore new secure architectures and coding practices.
Research and share methods for hardening or rewriting code with projects that want to go further than patching.
We’ll do this based on guidance from open-source maintainers and foundations, and share what works so other projects can replicate it. We started the AI for Science program in May 2025 with the belief that AI could significantly speed up scientific progress. Our goal is to increase access to AI tools and resources to enable researchers to deepen and expand their own scientific work. (Over the last few months, we’ve also launched our discounted
Team plan for scientists
and have supported hundreds of projects across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, climate science, and mathematics.)
Scientists have told us that they’re working with Claude to generate hypotheses, design experiments, swiftly analyze complex data, and communicate findings. With scientists at the center of this transformation, the field is setting the questions and developing the research projects that will help us tackle some of humanity’s toughest problems.

HHMI Janelia Research Campus
to develop the
Model Hardware Standard
(MHS), a shared specification that lets AI agents safely operate lab instruments. MHS is currently in research preview. We also support the
Allen Institute
, a leader in creating large open datasets and tools to advance research on the brain, cells, and the immune system. The institute is building teams of AI agents to analyze that data, turning months of manual analysis into hours.
AI for Science began by supporting individual scientists. By partnering with institutions and foundations, we’re now able to reach more researchers across many fields. Many of these projects will also produce public goods that benefit the wider scientific community: open datasets, open-source software, open standards, and shared libraries. We look forward to seeing how AI resources can expand what scientists can attempt and lead to new discoveries.
Science funders and societies
Science funders and societies play an enormous role in finding and funding original, high-impact projects. We’re sharing Claude credits with the following organizations, which will distribute these resources to ambitious researchers aiming to use AI for scientific research:
The Alfred P. Sloan Foundation.
Founded in 1934, it supports original research and education in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and economics.
The Simons Foundation.
This foundation advances the frontiers of research in mathematics and basic sciences through grants and its Flatiron Institute.
Schmidt Sciences.
Founded in 2024 by Eric and Wendy Schmidt, it works to accelerate scientific knowledge and breakthroughs with the most promising, advanced tools to support a thriving planet. The organization prioritizes research in areas poised for impact, including AI and advanced computing, astrophysics, biosciences, climate, and space—and supports researchers in a variety of disciplines through its science systems program.
Open Source for Science Fund, a program of Renaissance Philanthropy.
This is a time-bound philanthropic fund at Renaissance Philanthropy sustaining and evolving the open-source software stack that underpins science.
The US National Science Foundation.
This $9 billion federal agency established by Congress in 1950 promotes the progress of science, advances national health and defense, and funds competitive research and education, accounting for about 25% of federal support for basic research at US colleges and universities.
CAS, a division of the American Chemical Society.
For more than a century, CAS has indexed the world’s published chemistry, and it maintains the CAS REGISTRY®, the standard system for identifying chemical substances.
Institutions
Leading research institutions produce some of the world’s most important scientific advances, data, instruments, and tools. These institutional partners will use Claude credits inside their organizations to enable scientific discovery:
Space Telescope Science Institute.
STScI runs science operations for NASA’s Hubble, James Webb, and Roman space telescopes. Managed by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA), STScI also holds one of the largest astronomy data archives used by scientists worldwide.
Wellcome Sanger Institute.
One of the world’s leading genomics centers, it generates genomic and functional data at scale, with work that spans human genetics, biodiversity, and drug development.
The Francis Crick Institute.
Based in London, it’s one of Europe’s largest biomedical research institutes, with more than 100 research groups studying the biology behind health and disease.
Imperial College London, Department of Life Sciences.
One of Europe’s largest life science departments, it conducts research ranging from the structure of single molecules to whole ecosystems, with a focus on health, disease, and climate resilience.
EMBL.
The European Molecular Biology Laboratory is Europe’s intergovernmental life science laboratory, with six sites across the continent delivering both research and services across experimental and computational approaches in biology. EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) hosts a number of key open data resources that biologists use every day, such as Ensembl, Protein Data Bank in Europe, and Europe PMC.
Gladstone Institutes.
An independent biomedical research institute in San Francisco, it integrates AI and data science across its work on cardiology, neurology, infectious diseases, cancer, and autoimmune diseases.

As part of this work, we’re also continuing to support innovative research by providing Claude credits directly to specific research initiatives, focusing on problems with the potential for large public impact. The new projects are:
FlyWire, Princeton University (neuroscience).
It produced the first complete wiring map of an adult fruit fly’s brain and develops open data and tools for connectomics, enabling researchers to discover how neural circuits give rise to perception and behavior.
LEAP, Columbia University (Earth system).
Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics is a National Science Foundation center that combines machine learning with physics to improve how climate models capture clouds, oceans, and land.
AstroPath, Johns Hopkins University (cancer research).

gnomAD, Broad Institute (genomics and rare disease).
The Genome Aggregation Database pools DNA data from over 800,000 people into an open reference of human genetic variation that researchers and clinical labs around the world use to support rare disease discovery and diagnosis.
Tau Ceti (mathematics).
This open, community-driven project is building a shared autoformalized library of mathematics in Lean, a language that lets computers check every proof.
Centre for Population Genomics.
A joint initiative between Australia’s Garvan Institute of Medical Research and Murdoch Children’s Research Institute, it increases the inclusion of Australia’s multicultural communities in genomic resources and builds tools for rare disease diagnosis.
What’s next
Many of these collaborations are still in their early stages, and we’re eager to see how they can support novel research and scientific discovery. We look forward to sharing the impact of this work and showcasing new ways of working in these scientific fields.
As AI changes how science is done, our AI for Science program will continue to support and collaborate with scientists, institutions, and foundations. We hope to expand these efforts to even more partners around the world.

Barclays, the British universal bank, is expanding its strategic collaboration with Anthropic to integrate secure, enterprise-grade AI systems across its global operations.
Barclays is extending Claude across the bank to accelerate software development, modernize legacy systems, and improve operational efficiency. As part of this rollout, Barclays expects Claude Code adoption to reach 50% of its developer population by the end of 2026, rising to a majority of software engineers in 2027.
Barclays builds with Claude to better serve customers
Integrating AI across a large, complex, and highly regulated organization requires both capable technology and disciplined governance. Expanding its collaboration with Anthropic reflects a shared commitment to deploying AI responsibly, reliably, and in ways that deliver real outcomes, such as providing faster support for customers.
“The true measure of any technology is the impact it has on customers, clients, and colleagues, and the outcomes it enables,” said Anne Marie Darling, Group Co-Chief Operating Officer at Barclays. “Expanding the use of Claude across Barclays is about more than adopting AI. It is about transforming how work gets done: reimagining processes, enhancing customer and client experiences, and building a simpler, more efficient organization within a secure and well-governed environment. By reducing time spent on routine activities and streamlining decision-making, we can enable colleagues to focus their expertise where it matters most, solving more complex problems, accelerating innovation, and delivering better outcomes for our customers, clients, and business.”
“Software engineering and cyber security are both being reshaped by increasingly capable AI systems,” said Craig Bright, Group Co-Chief Operating Officer at Barclays. “We're moving towards AI as an increasingly agentic capability embedded within how we build, test, secure, and operate technology. At Barclays, we're using Claude to help modernize legacy platforms, improve software quality, and allow our technical experts to focus on the most complex challenges. The combination of skilled engineers, cyber specialists, and trusted AI capabilities has the potential to fundamentally improve how technology is developed and managed across large-scale enterprises.”
Claude powers knowledge assistance to speed up customer servicing
One example of the partnership already in action is Barclays’ Colleague Knowledge Assistant, which helps Barclays UK employees find information and answers more quickly when supporting their over 20 million UK retail customers.
The capability, which has been live since 2025, is powered by Claude through a retrieval-augmented generation architecture. More than 16,000 colleagues have adopted the assistant, and it has handled over one million searches.
The result is faster access to information and quicker support for customers.
Enhancing operational efficiency in Barclays’ Global Markets business
Within Barclays' Global Markets business, Claude models are helping streamline how client inquiries are processed and managed.
Teams use Claude models to classify, enrich, and determine the optimal processing route for incoming emails, helping to prioritize and ensure requests contain the information needed for operations colleagues to take action. The platform processes approximately 120,000 emails each day, reducing manual handling activity while helping colleagues identify and act on relevant information more efficiently.
Scaling AI responsibly
As Barclays continues to expand its use of AI, responsible deployment remains central to the partnership. The bank applies robust governance, security controls, and human oversight to AI use cases, ensuring technology is deployed safely and effectively across the organization.
“Our work with Barclays is a significant milestone for us in the UK. Barclays serves millions of customers and clients across the globe, so their standard for AI is high. That's why Barclays is rolling Claude out with strong security and oversight,” said Paul Smith, Chief Commercial Officer at Anthropic. “Claude now helps 16,000 Barclays’ colleagues find answers for customers, sorts 120,000 emails a day, and will be in the hands of most Barclays engineers by 2027. Very few institutions hold AI to such a high standard.”
Looking ahead
The expanded partnership reflects Barclays’ long-term commitment to using AI to improve productivity, strengthen resilience, and improve customer and client outcomes. By combining Anthropic’s frontier AI capabilities with Barclays’ focus on responsible innovation, the organizations are working together to scale practical AI applications across one of the world’s largest financial institutions.
